entityDossier.whatItIs: Los Alamos National Laboratory, the Department of Energy federally funded research and development centre at Los Alamos, New Mexico, administered by Triad National Security, LLC since 9 June 2018 and receiving approximately $3,918.3 million in FY2024. It is the laboratory that built the first nuclear weapons, and on this board it appears in three unrelated capacities: as the host of a documented 1949 conference on the green fireballs, as an institution whose own archivist says it fields several UFO-related FOIA requests a year, and as the workplace named in the single most contested credential claim in the subject.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: It joined this map with the Lazar cluster of 18 September 2026, and it is the node where that cluster's central factual question actually lives. Bob Lazar's account requires a documented scientific career, and the one contemporaneous document that appears to supply it is a Los Alamos artefact: the 27 June 1982 front page of the Los Alamos Monitor, which reports on him as a laboratory-connected physicist, and a 1982 internal telephone directory that lists his name. Both are real, both were opened, and both are narrower than the use made of them. The laboratory is therefore not a bystander here. It is the place where the strongest evidence for the claimant and the strongest qualification of that evidence sit on the same pair of pages.
entityDossier.narrative:
The board carries this laboratory for the ordinary reasons first. It hosted a conference on 16 February 1949 on the green fireballs, attended by Laboratory Director Norris Bradbury and Frederick Reines among others, which is documented by the laboratory itself rather than by the literature about it. Its senior archivist has said on the record that the institution receives several FOIA requests a year on unidentified aerial phenomena, which is a rare thing for an institution to say about itself and is the reason a `custody` reading of this node is defensible at all.

What brought it onto the top-level map is narrower and sharper. The Lazar account stands or falls on whether he was what he said he was, and the only contemporaneous documentary thread in his favour runs through here. On 27 June 1982 the Los Alamos Monitor put him on its front page. A 1982 internal telephone directory lists his name. Taken together they are routinely presented as proof of employment at the laboratory.

They are not that, and this node exists partly to say so precisely. The directory's own terms state that it covers outside contractors as well as staff, and a 1996 taped interview with a former colleague places him under Kirk-Mayer, a contractor, which is why `kirk-mayer` is now a node in its own right with an edge to this one. The board's rule, written as a claim on this node rather than left to a reader to work out, is that his connection is to be stated as named in a directory and never as employed by. That is a smaller claim than either his supporters or his critics usually make, and it is the one the documents support.

The laboratory has made no statement about him in anything opened here, and none is asserted. The edge from this node to `bob-lazar` is Tier 3 for exactly that reason.

claims.text: THE CONNECTION IS A DIRECTORY LISTING AND MUST NEVER BE STATED AS EMPLOYMENT. Bob Lazar appears in a 1982 Los Alamos telephone directory, and that directory's own terms state that it covers outside contractors in addition to laboratory staff. A 1996 taped interview with a former colleague places him under the contractor Kirk-Mayer. No employment record was opened. This board states the connection as 'named in a directory' and nothing more.
claims.source: The 1982 Los Alamos telephone directory listing and the 1996 taped colleague interview, as recorded in research/leads/verified-lazar-s4-2026-09-18.md, opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE CONTEMPORANEOUS ARTEFACT IS REAL AND IS NARROWER THAN ITS USE. The Los Alamos Monitor of 27 June 1982 carries him on its front page. It is a dated, openable, contemporaneous newspaper record and it is the strongest single thread in his favour. It is a local newspaper's account, not a personnel record, and it carries the same qualification as the directory.
claims.source: Los Alamos Monitor front page, 27 June 1982, opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE LABORATORY DOCUMENTS ITS OWN UAP HISTORY. LANL states that a conference was organised at Los Alamos on 16 February 1949 on the green fireballs, attended by Laboratory Director Norris Bradbury and Frederick Reines among others, and that its senior archivist receives several FOIA requests every year related to unidentified flying objects and other unexplained aerial phenomena.
claims.source: LANL's own published statements, already on the board before this cluster

openQuestions: The 1982 Los Alamos telephone directory page itself, as an image. It is described and quoted in the secondary literature but was not opened as a scan, so its exact wording and the placement of his entry are not established here.
Any laboratory or Kirk-Mayer personnel record for Bob Lazar. None was opened, and the board asserts no employment either way.
Whether the laboratory has ever made any statement about him. Nothing opened here contains one.

entityDossier.whatItIs: KLAS-TV, the CBS affiliate on Channel 8 in Las Vegas, and the originating institution of the Bob Lazar claim. Its reporter and news anchor George Knapp, who joined in 1981, broadcast the programmes in May and November 1989 that put Lazar and the name S-4 into public circulation. A Las Vegas Review-Journal report of 19 June 1990 records contemporaneously that Lazar was the focal point of those broadcasts, which is how the board dates them without having opened the broadcasts themselves.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: A local television newsroom is on this map because the modern subject has a traceable point of origin and this is it. Almost everything the board carries downstream of 1989 about S-4, about element 115 and about a reverse-engineering programme at a Nevada site descends from a sequence of reports on one CBS affiliate. The station is not a commentator on this story. It is the custody point for the story's first public form, and the board treats it the way it treats any custodian: the institution that held and released a claim, distinct from the claim's truth.
entityDossier.narrative:
The reason this node matters more than its size suggests is that the board can date the 1989 broadcasts only indirectly. The broadcasts themselves were not opened. What was opened is a Las Vegas Review-Journal report of 19 June 1990 which records, contemporaneously and for its own unrelated reasons, that Lazar had been the focal point of KLAS reporting. That is why `klas-lazar-broadcasts-1989` is built as a deliberately thin node anchored on a 1990 newspaper line with its air dates carried at Tier 3, rather than as a confident record of what aired and when.

That thinness is the honest state of the evidence and it should not be quietly improved. The station's own archive was not reached, and three attempts to open the successor site returned HTTP 403. A session that opens a 1989 artefact will be able to move several Tier 3 claims in this cluster to Tier 1 in a single stroke, and that is the highest-value gap in it.

The station's later role is separate and better documented. Knapp's reporting is one of the routes by which the AAWSAP contract and the Reid correspondence reached the public record, which is why this node carries edges to `aawsap`, `harry-reid` and `james-lacatski` alongside the Lazar ones. It is a newsroom that has been the first public custodian of this subject twice, thirty years apart.

claims.text: THIS IS THE ORIGINATING INSTITUTION OF THE LAZAR CLAIM, AND THE DATING IS INDIRECT. The Bob Lazar programmes aired on KLAS in May and November 1989, and a Las Vegas Review-Journal report of 19 June 1990 records contemporaneously that Lazar was the focal point of that reporting. The broadcasts themselves were not opened by any session on this board.
claims.source: Las Vegas Review-Journal, 19 June 1990, opened 2026-09-18; the 1989 air dates are carried at Tier 3 on klas-lazar-broadcasts-1989

claims.text: THE REPORTER IS DOCUMENTED AND THE TENURE IS DATED. George Knapp joined KLAS-TV as reporter and news anchor in 1981, left in 1991, and was rehired in 1995.
claims.source: Already on the board before this cluster

openQuestions: ANY 1989 ARTEFACT OF THE BROADCASTS THEMSELVES. None has been opened by any session. The station's successor site returned HTTP 403 on three attempts. This is the highest-value single gap in the Lazar cluster: one opened 1989 recording or transcript would move several Tier 3 claims to Tier 1 at once.
Whether the station retains an archive of the May and November 1989 broadcasts, and whether it is reachable.
Whether John Lear was the route by which the story reached Knapp, which is widely asserted and was not established.
